proposals.name: Self-positioning as one more alternative among existing answers
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the answer text itself announces that it is an additional or alternative contribution sitting alongside other answers already present. 10 = the opening or framing explicitly marks it as supplementary: phrases like 'another approach', 'yet another way', 'here is a second answer', 'the other answers are too complicated', 'this is not an answer to the question but a complement to X', 'I post this separately from my first post'. 5 = a passing acknowledgement that other material exists but the answer is otherwise framed as standing on its own. 0 = the answer opens directly on the mathematics with no reference of any kind to other answers, other posts, or its own place in a sequence.
proposals.rationale: This is the single most consistent surface feature of the dense-low half. R27 opens 'The other answers are way too complicated for this particular problem'; R50 opens 'This is not an answer to the question but a complement to the Robert Israel's answer'; R47 opens 'Here is more standard way'; R48 opens 'Another approach'; R11 opens 'Here is an another proof'; R28 opens 'Here is yet another way, in case you are interested'; R35 opens 'Yet another approach'. All are card-high (0.67-0.99) and dense-low (0.02-0.34). The scorecard reads only the mathematics, which is genuinely clean, and cannot see that the text is self-declaring as a late addition to a question whose asker was already served. Contrast R33 and R41, which open on the computation and are dense-high with card near floor.

proposals.name: Direct verdict on the asker's own displayed work
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer explicitly adjudicates the attempt the asker showed in the question: states whether it is right or wrong, and if wrong, points at the specific step that fails. 10 = an unambiguous verdict plus localisation ('your computation is correct, but the chain rule is simpler'; 'it should be used, there may be some little mistakes in your computation' followed by the corrected chain; 'if you are enumerating everyone's birthday in the denominator then for each term you need to multiply by ...'). 5 = the answer engages the asker's method implicitly by redoing it, but never renders a verdict. 0 = the answer never refers to the asker's attempt at all and simply presents its own independent development.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('So your work is correct'), R20 ('It should be used. There may be some little mistakes in your computation'), R22 ('Your computation looks fine. I don't think there is an easier way'), R55 ('Your DFA looks good to me') and R49 (locating exactly which factor the asker's enumeration omits) are all dense-high with card at or near the floor (0.005-0.207). R22 in particular is two sentences of pure adjudication and scores card 0.051 against dense 0.790. A criterion bank built on mathematical content has nothing to reward here, because the value delivered is a verdict, not a derivation.

proposals.name: Deliverable ambition matched to the question's ambition
proposals.instruction: Judge the fit between the size of the thing asked for and the size of the thing delivered. 10 = the answer delivers exactly the object the question names and then stops. 5 = the answer delivers what was asked plus a moderate generalisation. 0 = severe mismatch in either direction: a narrow computational question answered with a research-scale program, a long treatise with announced future instalments, or a general theory developed where a single instance was requested. Judge only against what the question text asks for, not against the intrinsic quality of the mathematics.
proposals.rationale: R01 asks for a constructive proof and receives a partial programme prefaced with 'I have a plan for a much larger blog post, but it is an ambitious one so it may be several months until I get to write it', then proves only the regular-prime case; card 0.955, dense 0.232. R46 asks for a simple independence proof and receives a forcing tutorial with poset and generic-filter definitions; card 0.949, dense 0.323. R43 (card 0.183, dense 0.820) shows the other direction working in the dense model's favour: it generalises but reaches the asked-for number 102 explicitly first. The scorecard rewards breadth as thoroughness; the dense model appears to treat unrequested breadth as drift away from the asker.

proposals.name: Second-person address with an executable next step
proposals.instruction: Score how directly the answer speaks to the asker and hands them something to do. 10 = sustained second-person address plus a concrete instruction the asker can execute immediately ('Now you can solve for x using inverse trigonometric functions'; 'Apply Menelaus in triangles ABD, CBF, ...'; 'You try one: what is 9:51 divided by two?'). 5 = occasional second-person but no actionable step. 0 = entirely impersonal third-person exposition addressed to no one in particular.
proposals.rationale: R26 (dense 0.814, card 0.018) is a four-line hint ending 'Now you can solve for x'; R24 (dense 0.768, card 0.035) is a single sentence naming the six triangles to apply the theorem in; R51 (dense 0.981, card 0.261) teaches a procedure, works three examples, sets a practice problem and supplies the answer at the end. All three sit near the top of dense and near the bottom of card. Against these, R44 and R45 are impersonal and polished and land card 0.976 and 0.917 with dense 0.148 and 0.084. A criterion bank scoring rigour cannot register address.

proposals.name: Disparagement of the asker or of rival answers
proposals.instruction: Score how much the text belittles the asker's competence or other answers. 10 = overt disparagement: telling the asker they are overcomplicating a trivial thing, recommending they use a calculator engine instead of thinking, calling other answers overkill or way too complicated, declaring the question's premise to contain less than meets the eye. 5 = mild corrective framing that still respects the asker or the other answer. 0 = no disparagement anywhere; disagreements with other material are stated neutrally and technically.
proposals.rationale: R23 (dense 0.077, card 0.788) opens 'You are overcomplicating it' and closes 'For future, try using WolframAlpha for basic integrals'. R27 (dense 0.043, card 0.863) opens by declaring the other answers 'way too complicated' and 'completely overkill', then adds a scolding edit 'or I'll just do it for you myself, since you seem to think it leads to another recurrence'. R53 (dense 0.076, card 0.838) tells the asker their observation is 'a case where there is less than meets the eye' and concludes 'In general...none'. R58 and R56 open by improving on or correcting another answer. The mathematics in all of these is correct and compact, which is exactly why the scorecard scores them high.

proposals.name: Machinery level far above the question's evident level
proposals.instruction: Score the gap between the sophistication of the tools invoked and the sophistication the question displays. 10 = an extreme gap, e.g. a routine power-series expansion handled through the Faa di Bruno formula and partial Bell polynomials with a literature reference list, or an elementary infinite product routed through Jacobi theta functions and zeta values. 5 = tools one clear step above what the question shows but still the natural ones. 0 = tools drawn from exactly the toolkit the question itself displays. This is a measure of gap, not of correctness or elegance.
proposals.rationale: R16 (dense 0.772, card 0.093) answers a standard binomial series expansion with Bell polynomials plus three journal citations, and the dense model marks it down while the card presumably marks it down too, but far harder. The reverse direction is more telling: R09 (dense 0.097, card 0.994) reaches theta functions and zeta(3/2) for a product analysis and gets essentially the top card score; R44 (dense 0.148, card 0.976) and R45 (dense 0.084, card 0.917) do the same with equivariant immersions and Poincare-Hopf. R31 (dense 0.057) and R33 (dense 0.867) are both elementary, so level alone is not the story: the criterion must be scored as gap relative to the question.

proposals.name: Hint that names the exact tool and its exact point of application
proposals.instruction: Score the quality of the answer as a hint, applying this only where the answer deliberately withholds the full derivation. 10 = the withheld derivation is replaced by a precise, immediately usable pointer: the named theorem and the specific objects to apply it to, or a first line of algebra that visibly opens the problem, or a hint with the full proof supplied in a spoiler beneath it. 3 = a vague nudge that names a topic but not a move. 0 = the answer gives no hint and no derivation, or the hint would not let a competent reader proceed. Score 5 if the answer is a full derivation, i.e. the criterion does not apply.
proposals.rationale: R24 is one sentence naming Menelaus and the six triangles, and scores dense 0.768 against card 0.035. R26 is four lines of algebra reaching tan x = -1 and stopping, dense 0.814 against card 0.018. R17 gives a one-line reframing ('a disguised version of the Schroder-Bernstein theorem') and then hides a full proof below, dense 0.931 against card 0.339. R15 opens 'The following may get you started' and delivers both marginal densities, dense 0.922 against card 0.052. A bank that scores completeness will punish all four as incomplete; the dense model appears to price the precision of the pointer instead.

proposals.name: Mid-answer thread residue addressed to named third parties
proposals.instruction: Score the presence of accreted conversational material inside the answer body that is addressed to someone other than the asker. 10 = several such markers: edits headed with another user's name, priority disclaimers acknowledging that someone else got there first, thanks to a named commenter whose suggestion the answer follows, or attribution of the idea to a named person in the comments. 5 = one such marker. 0 = the body contains no named third parties and no edit apparatus.
proposals.rationale: R13 (dense 0.341, card 0.993) carries 'EDIT 1. (To Asaf Shachar)' and 'EDIT 2. To @ Asaf Shachar. Now I prove (with the help of a colleague)'. R09 (dense 0.097, card 0.994) ends with a Disclaimer acknowledging 'Semiclassical got there first'. R40 (dense 0.223, card 0.975) opens 'This is expanding on a comment by Bill'. R45 (dense 0.084, card 0.917) says 'as suggested by Ted'. R58 (dense 0.134, card 0.822) opens '@supinf showed us a nice set of examples'. This is distinct from A01: A01 is about the opening frame, this is about material that grew inside the post while a discussion was already underway. The two highest card scores in the whole slice both carry it.

proposals.name: Authorial hedging about the answer's own validity
proposals.instruction: Score how provisional the author sounds about their own claim. 10 = heavily hedged: 'the following might work', 'if I remember right', 'I don't know what you mean', 'no promise that they will be helpful', 'the third and fourth are discutable', 'I think it is important to state', explicit statements that only part of the claim was proved. 5 = one softening qualifier over an otherwise firm claim. 0 = the claim is asserted flatly and the derivation is presented as settled.
proposals.rationale: R40 (dense 0.223, card 0.975) says 'the following might work' and 'if I remember right, the Jensen inequality for Log reads'. R50 (dense 0.027, card 0.959) calls two of its four envelope solutions 'discutable (not given by WA)'. R30 (dense 0.096, card 0.801) is framed throughout as 'I think it is important to state that'. R53 (dense 0.076) says 'imho'. R13 admits in EDIT 1 that 'I proved only that the equation f(x)=1 has at least one solution' before a later edit repairs it. A criterion bank scoring the mathematics sees the finished chain and not the author's own uncertainty about it.

proposals.name: Substance in the first two lines versus long preamble
proposals.instruction: Score how quickly the answer reaches the load-bearing content. 10 = the first sentence already contains the decisive object: the verdict, the counterexample, the key identity, the definition asked for. 5 = one short orienting sentence before the substance. 0 = several paragraphs of framing, meta-commentary about the answer's own provenance, or scene-setting before anything decisive appears.
proposals.rationale: R34 (dense 0.740, card 0.032) is a single line exhibiting A = R-infinity, B = R, C = R-squared and is done. R29 (dense 0.874, card 0.122) states 'This is not possible' and gives the spectrum argument in four lines. R21 (dense 0.883, card 0.257) is one displayed chain. R33 and R41 likewise. Against these, R01 spends three paragraphs on its own scope and future blog post before the first claim, and R60 spends its opening on which edition of a book the author has in front of them; both are dense-low. The card scores of the fast-opening group cluster between 0.03 and 0.26, so the bank is systematically reading brevity as thinness.

proposals.name: Diagnosis of the misconception behind the question
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer explains why the asker's own reasoning went where it did, as opposed to merely presenting a correct route. 10 = the answer names the specific false step or hidden assumption and explains the mechanism ('your method isn't counting scenarios like two pairs of people each of whom have the same birthday'; an explicit construction of the map that shows why forgetting individual identity preserves uniformity, followed by an anti-example where it fails). 5 = the correct route is given and the contrast with the asker's route is left implicit. 0 = no engagement with why the confusion arose.
proposals.rationale: R49 (dense 0.952, card 0.187) does nothing but this: it explains the missing multiplier and then adds that even repaired, the method miscounts double-pairs. R12 (dense 0.960, card 0.359) constructs the map from labelled orderings to red/blue marbles, shows every preimage has size 10, and then supplies an anti-example where the preimages have unequal size so the same shortcut fails. Both are top-decile dense with card in the bottom third. R20 (dense 0.788, card 0.024) is a milder case. The value here is causal explanation of an error, which a rubric of mathematical-quality criteria will not have a slot for.

proposals.name: Works inside the asker's own notation and setup
proposals.instruction: Score notational and structural continuity with the question. 10 = the answer reuses the asker's symbols, their stated setup and their intermediate expressions, so that the reader can lay it directly over their own page. 5 = mostly the asker's notation with some new symbols introduced and defined. 0 = the answer discards the question's formulation and rebuilds the problem in its own formalism before starting.
proposals.rationale: R05 (dense 0.899, card 0.166), R06 (dense 0.941, card 0.344), R10 (dense 0.903, card 0.086) and R39 (dense 0.816, card 0.023) all stay entirely inside the question's own variables and setup. Against these, R44 (dense 0.148, card 0.976) rebuilds the problem as an orthogonal-group action with new notation macros; R35 (dense 0.044, card 0.732) introduces a Fitch-diagram macro and renders the whole proof inside it; R13 (dense 0.341, card 0.993) opens by declaring 'This is not a question about linear algebra' and re-founds the problem. Reformulation reads as strength to a content rubric and as distance from the asker to the dense model.

proposals.name: Pointer to a named external resource that actually closes the question
proposals.instruction: Score the usefulness of any redirection outside the answer. 10 = the answer names a specific external resource together with enough in-text work to make the pointer land, e.g. identifying the asker's integer sequence in the OEIS by catalogue number and describing what is found there. 5 = a relevant resource named but the reader must do the matching themselves. 0 = either a vague redirection with no locator ('my colleague wrote some notes, I don't have the URL handy'), a redirection that substitutes for reasoning the asker asked for ('try using WolframAlpha for basic integrals'), or bare unlabelled links. Score 5 if the answer contains no external pointer.
proposals.rationale: R32 (dense 0.816 in the high half at 0.807, card 0.144) does nothing but identify the sequence as OEIS A038534 and describe what is there, and the dense model ranks it high while the card ranks it near the floor. R55 (dense 0.754, card 0.101) is the weak version, naming a colleague's unlocatable notes, and still sits dense-high. R23 (dense 0.077, card 0.788) is the harmful version, telling the asker to use WolframAlpha next time. The bank appears to penalise any redirection uniformly, whereas the direction of the effect in this slice depends on whether the pointer resolves the question.

proposals.name: Elementary question closed completely in a handful of lines
proposals.instruction: Composite. Score high only when both halves hold: the question is elementary or narrowly computational, AND the answer carries it to a fully determined final object with every step shown and nothing left dangling. 10 = both, e.g. a chain of exponent rules ending at a single power, or a sum of n copies of a term evaluated to na, or a factorisation ending at a specific numeric total. 5 = elementary question but with a gap or an unjustified jump. 0 = either the question is not elementary, or the answer leaves the final object undetermined.
proposals.rationale: R33 (dense 0.867, card 0.121), R41 (dense 0.918, card 0.316), R21 (dense 0.883, card 0.257) and R59 (dense 0.872, card 0.185) are all of this shape and all sit high-dense with card in the bottom third: the card model has no way to credit an answer whose entire merit is that it is short, complete and exactly right. The composite is needed because shortness alone is not the signal: R19 answers the same question as R59 with an unexplained list of six numbers and scores dense 0.742, below R59's 0.872, while R38 reaches the same total through a partly garbled argument ('not divisible by 3 because they are divisible by 3') at dense 0.834 and card 0.004.

proposals.name: Discovery narration paired with respect for the asker
proposals.instruction: Composite of two interacting properties. First, narration: does the author think aloud, marking the moment an idea arrives, inviting the reader to look at an equation, exclaiming at a step. Second, stance: is the narration directed at bringing the asker along or at showing that the problem was beneath the author. 10 = strong narration in a companionable stance, walking through the discovery and inviting the asker to try one. 5 = flat exposition with no narration and no disparagement. 0 = strong narration in a dismissive stance, where the thinking-aloud exists to dramatise how easy the author finds it.
proposals.rationale: R51 (dense 0.981, card 0.261) narrates the base-60 halving trick, works three examples, and hands the asker a practice problem, closing 'I hope this was helpful'. R03 (dense 0.658, card 0.013) narrates enthusiastically ('AHAAA!') at the asker's side even though the derivation is wrong, and the dense model still places it above the middle while the card places it at 0.013. The negative pole is R27 (dense 0.043, card 0.863), whose narration is 'Just look at this equation for a few seconds' and 'Notice you don't need any linear algebra, eigenvectors, or other higher-level math', and R23 (dense 0.077, card 0.788) with 'Well, jolly gosh!'. Narration and stance must be scored jointly because narration alone appears on both sides of the split.

proposals.name: Latecomer framing: presupposes other answers already exist
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer text presupposes that other answers, comments, or prior discussion of this same question already exist at the time of writing. Count explicit markers ('another approach', 'yet another way', 'the other answer', 'this is expanding on a comment by X', 'I post this answer separately', 'this is not an answer but a complement to', 'the other answers are way too complicated'), and also implicit ones (positioning the contribution as an alternative, shorter, more elementary, or corrective variant of something unnamed). 0 = the text engages the raw question from scratch with no trace that anything had been said; 10 = the opening sentence itself is entirely about the existing answer stream. Score only how much of this framing is PRESENT. Do NOT judge whether referring to other answers is good, humble, useful, or bad practice, and do not judge the mathematics.
proposals.rationale: This is a pure arrival-order fingerprint, not a property of the mathematics: R03 opens 'Along the same lines as the other answer', R05 'Here is yet another way, in case you are interested', R55 'The other answers are way too complicated for this particular problem', R20 'Yet another approach', R58 'The other answer has roughly the right idea', R51 'This is not an answer to the question but a complement to the Robert Israel's answer'. Position in the stream is causally upstream of both the marker and of how an item fares, so the marker can carry predictive weight that has nothing to do with the answer's content. Tagged mixed because a genuinely later answerer can read the earlier ones and write something better-targeted.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (how many answers had already been posted when this one was written)

proposals.name: Second-person address to the asker's own work
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text is addressed to the specific person who asked, and engages that person's own posted attempt, rather than being written impersonally for a general future reader. Look for second-person pronouns tied to the asker's work ('your computation', 'your DFA', 'what you did', 'you are overcomplicating it', 'if you are enumerating...'), verdicts on the asker's own steps, and diagnosis of where the asker went wrong. 0 = no second-person address and no reference to any attempt by the asker; 10 = the entire text is a direct commentary on the asker's own posted work. Score presence and density only. Do NOT judge whether addressing the asker is helpful, courteous, or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 trace. R07 ends 'So your work is correct'; R11 opens 'Your DFA looks good to me'; R31 'It should be used. There may be some little mistakes in your computation'; R33 is only 'Your computation looks fine'; R48 'If you are enumerating everyone's birthday in the denominator...'. Whether prose is aimed at one asker or at the archive is an authorial stance, not a measure of mathematical content -- R33 addresses the asker in two sentences with no mathematics at all. Tagged mixed because targeting the asker's actual confusion can also be genuinely more responsive.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's relationship to the reader (writing for this one asker versus for the audience of future searchers)

proposals.name: Hint register and deliberate incompleteness
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text presents itself as a partial nudge rather than a completed derivation: literal 'Hint:' labels, 'this may get you started', 'now you can solve for x', 'I'll leave the last step to you', a named theorem or trick offered without carrying it through, or a proof deliberately hidden/withheld. 0 = fully worked from premise to conclusion with nothing left to the reader; 10 = the text is nothing but a pointer or a single suggested tool. Score the extent of the hint register only. Do NOT judge whether withholding the full solution is pedagogically good or bad, and do not judge whether the hint is correct.
proposals.rationale: R37 is a bare 'Hint: Apply Melanaus theorem...' one-liner; R39 is 'Hint:' plus three lines and 'Now you can solve for x'; R08 opens 'Hint:' and hides the proof in a spoiler block; R56 opens 'The following may get you started'; R55 says 'I'll leave the last step of simplifying the summation to you'. Hint register is a venue-norm habit that varies with the answerer's site experience and with the perceived homework-status of the question, and it is scorable purely from surface framing. Tagged mixed because calibrated hinting can genuinely serve the reader.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's practice with site homework-policy conventions (a regular who knows the norm of hinting rather than solving)

proposals.name: Bulk, display-math density and sectioning load
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of sheer textual and typographic bulk: total length, number of separate display-math blocks and multi-line aligned environments, presence of headed sections, numbered claims, bulleted or enumerated lists, boxed results, tabular arrays, and references to figures or plots. 0 = a couple of lines with at most one inline formula; 10 = many screens of alternating prose and display mathematics with internal structure such as named Claims, Definitions or Cases. Count the apparatus; do NOT judge whether the length or structure is warranted, well-organised, or excessive.
proposals.rationale: Bulk is trivially machine-visible and varies enormously across the slice independently of what is being established: R29 is two lines, R14 one display line, R45 one aligned block, R54 two sentences; against R30 (many sections, Claim 1, Claim 2, custom macros), R42 (multiple Definitions and an outlined construction), R16, R24 and R28 (screens of display work, figure references). A text-only model can latch on to volume as a proxy for effort or seriousness without that volume tracking whether the asker's own need was met.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: MathJax/markup fluency and custom macro use
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of practised, site-specific markup craft visible in the source: user-defined macros declared inline (\def, \newcommand), tagged and labelled equations (\tag, \label, \eqref), hand-built array/align/pmatrix environments, boxed or bbox-highlighted terms, colour commands, spacing hacks (\hspace, \quad, \;, \!), spoiler-hidden blocks, and consistent use of blackboard-bold/script font commands. 0 = plain text with at most naive dollar-sign inline math; 10 = the answer opens with a macro preamble and uses several distinct advanced markup facilities. Score the extent of markup machinery only. Do NOT judge whether the rendering is attractive, readable, or well chosen.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 fingerprint of an unseen factor (reputation/tenure) that leaves an unmistakable textual trace. R30 opens with '\def\QQ{\mathbb{Q}}\def\ZZ...\def\Gal...'; R20 defines an entire \fitch macro to draw a natural-deduction box; R38 declares '\newcommand{\O}{\mathcal{O}}'; R42 declares \Dom and \Rng; R32 uses \tag and \label with \eqref cross-references; R12 uses \fbox and \bbox borders. Contrast R25 and R26, which write '9! = 1 x 2 x 3' and bare implication lines with no math markup at all. Tenure predicts reception through channels other than content, so the trace must be declared a nuisance; tagged mixed because practised typesetters are often also practised expositors.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's standing and tenure on the site (a long-practised regular's typesetting habits versus a first-time poster's)

proposals.name: Post-hoc revision layering: EDIT blocks and addenda
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text shows evidence of having been returned to and extended after first publication: literal 'EDIT', 'Edit:', 'EDIT 1', 'EDIT 2', 'edit:' markers, appended sections addressing a named interlocutor, 'to clarify my comments above', disclaimers or acknowledgements appended at the end, parenthetical pointers such as 'please see comment below', and 'I just read your last post'. 0 = a single uninterrupted composition with no revision trace; 10 = multiple explicitly labelled edit layers appended over time. Score the visible revision trace only. Do NOT judge whether editing improved the answer or whether the edits were necessary.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. The unseen factor -- an answer that attracted enough back-and-forth for its author to keep working on it -- leaves a hard textual mark. R23 carries 'EDIT 1. (To Asaf Shachar)' and 'EDIT 2. To @ Asaf Shachar. Now I prove (with the help of a colleague)'; R09 has a bare 'EDIT' before the long calculation; R11 has 'EDIT: I have three suggestions'; R55 has 'Edit: or I'll just do it for you myself, since you seem to think...'; R12 opens 'To clarify my comments above'; R24 closes with a 'Disclaimer' acknowledging priority; R28 notes '(now validated by Prof. Shifrin)'. Attention begets edits, so the edit trace is downstream of attention, not of intrinsic content. Mixed because a revised answer may genuinely be a corrected, more complete one.
proposals.upstream_parent: post-publication thread dynamics and elapsed dwell time (the answerer returning to respond to comments and objections)

proposals.name: Named participants, @handles and priority acknowledgements
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text names or tags other people in the thread or beyond it: @-handles, first names or usernames of other answerers and commenters, 'the OP' as a term of art, credit assignments ('as suggested by X', 'X got there first', 'expanding on a comment by X', 'with the help of a colleague'), and appeals to a named authority who reviewed the work. 0 = no person is named or tagged anywhere; 10 = several named participants are addressed or credited throughout. Score naming density only. Do NOT judge whether the credit is generous, deserved, or well placed.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Social embedding is unobservable but leaves handles in the text. R34 opens '@supinf showed us a nice set of examples'; R12 refers to '@ReihardMeier's answer'; R23 addresses 'Asaf Shachar' twice; R09 credits 'a comment by Bill'; R10 opens 'Clive's answer is already a good one'; R57 'as suggested by Ted'; R24 'I acknowledge that Semiclassical got there first'; R28 'now validated by Prof. Shifrin'; R21 and R51 use 'OP' and name 'Robert Israel'. Being on first-name terms with the regulars is a standing/network property and is not a property of the answer's substance, so it is a declared nuisance rather than a mixed channel.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's social embedding in the site community (recognising and being recognised by other regulars)

proposals.name: Routine-exercise register versus specialist-research register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for where the QUESTION-AND-ANSWER pair sits on a register axis visible in the vocabulary and objects handled. Score low (0-3) when the material is standard first-courses fare with a single numeric or closed-form target (elementary differentiation, factoring an integer, summation identities, basic trigonometric extrema, multiple-choice options). Score high (7-10) when the material uses specialist vocabulary and machinery of a graduate or research register (forcing and generic filters, cyclotomic fields and Galois cohomology, Poincare-Hopf, partial Bell polynomials, Jacobi theta functions, tensor products of covector spaces). Score the register of the subject matter only. Do NOT judge whether the answer is difficult, impressive, or correct, and do NOT reward advanced topics.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4. The slice is strongly stratified on this axis and the axis is a property of the question, not of the answer: routine at R07 (differentiate e^{ax^3}), R29 (sum of n copies of a), R45 (2^45 arithmetic), R39 (extrema of sin^2 cos^2), R54 (list six numbers); specialist at R30 (Kronecker-Weber for regular primes), R42 (Levy collapse and generic filters), R57 (Euler characteristic via Poincare-Hopf), R53 (Faa di Bruno and partial Bell polynomials). Question kind governs how many answers arrive and who writes them, so any register signal a text-only model picks up is a container property leaking in, not evidence about this answer.
proposals.upstream_parent: the kind of question the answer is attached to (a routine homework computation versus a conceptual question that draws a crowd of expert answerers)

proposals.name: Informal voice: exclamations, sign-offs, emoticons, orthographic slips
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of informal, chatty or non-standard authorial voice: exclamation marks and exclamation runs, interjections ('AHAAA!', 'Well, jolly gosh!', 'Done!'), emoticons or kaomoji, closing pleasantries and personal sign-offs ('Cheers!', 'I hope this helps', '-Shahar', 'I hope this was helpful'), direct quizzing of the reader ('You try one'), first-person meta-commentary about the writer's own feelings or memory ('if I remember right', 'which I find easier to understand', 'imho'), and visible spelling or grammar slips ('imediatelly', 'althouth', 'conlude', 'polynom', 'finit'). 0 = uniformly impersonal, standard, edited prose; 10 = several distinct informality or slip markers. Score presence only. Do NOT judge whether informality is charming or unprofessional, and do NOT penalise or reward non-native English.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2: authorship is unseen, but register and orthography are its visible residue. R35 has 'AHAAA!' and closes '...as our answer!!!!!'; R36 has 'Well, jolly gosh!', 'Cheers!' and the sign-off '-Shahar'; R15 closes 'I hope this helps ^_^'; R43 closes 'I hope this was helpful,' and quizzes 'You try one'; R18 ends 'Done!'; R09 writes 'imediatelly' and 'if I remember right'; R13 'althouth'; R17 'conlude'; R32 'polynom'; R04 'imho' and 'pulbacks'. None of these bear on whether the answer resolved the asker's problem, but all are easy correlates of author identity.
proposals.upstream_parent: who produced it -- the author's writing background, English fluency and habitual register in this format

proposals.name: External-resource citation and tool appeals
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer routes authority outside itself: hyperlinks or URLs, named databases and their identifiers (OEIS sequence numbers), computer-algebra appeals ('confirmed by Wolfram Alpha', 'try using WolframAlpha'), numbered theorem citations to named textbooks ('theorem 12.29 of Rudin's Functional Analysis'), formal bibliography entries with journals and DOIs, named editions of books, pointers to lecture notes, and 'see this link / this post'. 0 = wholly self-contained with no outward pointer; 10 = the substance is largely a set of pointers plus a formal reference list. Score the extent of outward pointing only. Do NOT judge whether the citations are authoritative, relevant, or well formatted.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. R15 is essentially a pointer to OEIS A038534 plus 'In this post there are references to formulas'; R53 appends three journal references with DOIs; R24 says 'This result is confirmed by Wolfram Alpha'; R36 advises 'For future, try using WolframAlpha for basic integrals'; R41 cites 'theorem 12.29 of Rudin's Functional Analysis'; R11 points at a colleague's unlinked course notes; R27 cites 'Dr. Stewart's 1996 edition of from here to infinity' and links 'lexicographic ordering is not a well ordering'. Citation habit tracks who the author is and what they have at hand rather than whether the answer met the asker's need; tagged mixed because a well-sourced pointer can itself be exactly what was wanted.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's access to and practice with external resources and literature (academic affiliation, tooling habits)

proposals.name: Direct verdict on the asker's own posted work
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly evaluates the specific reasoning, computation, or attempt the asker posted in their question -- confirming it is correct, or pinpointing exactly where and why it goes wrong (e.g. naming a specific step, line, or substitution the asker used). Score 0 if the answer never engages with anything the asker specifically wrote or tried, and instead addresses only the abstract problem.
proposals.rationale: Rows R11 ('So your work is correct'), R31 ('your method isn't counting scenarios like...'), R33 ('Your DFA looks good to me'), and R47 ('There may be some little mistakes in your computation') all directly assess the asker's own attempt and sit in dense_high_card_low; this kind of direct engagement may be exactly what the dense model perceives and the scorecard undervalues.

proposals.name: Terse-and-conclusive delivery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer is short (reaches its point in a few lines) AND ends with an unambiguous, explicitly stated final result (a number, a closed-form expression, or a clear closing statement like 'Done' or a restated conclusion). Score 0 if the answer is long-form and/or never crisply lands on a stated final result, trailing off into further discussion, caveats, or an unfinished derivation.
proposals.rationale: R26 ends with 'Done!' after a short derivation and R59 closes on a boxed final fraction, both dense_high_card_low; by contrast R01 and R38 (dense_low_card_high) are long and end mid-discussion without a crisp closing statement.

proposals.name: Self-positioned as supplement to another answer
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly frames itself in relation to another answer on the thread -- e.g. 'another way', 'yet another approach', 'a complement to X's answer', 'this second answer'. Score 0 if the answer reads as a free-standing, first-line response with no reference to alternative or prior answers.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('not an answer... but a complement to the Robert Israel's answer'), R16 ('This second answer gives a shorter proof'), R24 ('Another option is to use'), and R40 ('Here is yet another way') are all dense_low_card_high, suggesting this self-positioning as secondary is something the scorecard rewards but that predicts low acceptance likelihood.

proposals.name: Named reference to another community member
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly names or @-mentions another user, commenter, or specific individual as a source, collaborator, or point of comparison. Score 0 if no person is named or referenced anywhere in the text.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('expanding on a comment by Bill'), R30 ('@iam_agf has the other'), R44 ('I acknowledge that Semiclassical got there first'), and R52 ('@supinf showed us a nice set of examples') are all dense_low_card_high, indicating visible embeddedness in a multi-answer social thread rather than a stand-alone top response.

proposals.name: Meta-commentary on the act of answering
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer contains explicit remarks about itself as a piece of writing or about the answering process -- e.g. why it was posted separately, plans for future write-ups, or personal provenance of a source consulted. Score 0 if the text contains no such self-referential commentary and addresses only the mathematics.
proposals.rationale: R14 ('I have Dr. Stewart's 1996 edition... in front of me now'), R36 ('I have a plan for a much larger blog post'), and R44 ('I post this answer separately, so that the analytics are not lost') are all dense_low_card_high, suggesting this kind of self-referential framing correlates with what the scorecard rewards but dense discounts.

proposals.name: Bare formal derivation without prose scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer is dominated by symbolic notation or formal proof steps (e.g. a Fitch-style natural-deduction derivation, or a chain of equations) with little or no connecting English explaining why each step is taken. Score 0 if every symbolic step is wrapped in plain-English narration guiding the reader through the reasoning.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R39, both nearly pure Fitch-notation natural-deduction proofs of the same problem with almost no prose, are dense_low_card_high, contrasting with prose-driven answers like R31 and R54 (dense_high_card_low) that narrate every step in plain language.

proposals.name: Hedged self-assessment of the proposed solution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly signals uncertainty about whether its own reasoning or result is complete or correct -- phrases like 'might work', 'I think this can be simplified', 'to my knowledge', 'not convinced yet?'. Score 0 if the answer asserts its own result with unqualified confidence throughout.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('the following might work') and R52 ('I think the proof can be simplified') both hedge about their own solution's adequacy and are dense_low_card_high, unlike confidently asserted answers such as R26 or R51 (dense_high_card_low).

proposals.name: Concrete worked numeric example anchoring the solution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core of the answer is carried by plugging in specific numbers or a specific small case and computing an explicit numeric result. Score 0 if the answer remains entirely at the level of general symbols or abstract structures with no concrete numeric instantiation.
proposals.rationale: R03, R09, and R18 all work the same question down to the concrete numeric answer '5+35=40', and R54 anchors an abstract probability argument in a labeled 7-seat example; all are dense_high_card_low, unlike the abstract general treatments in R01 or R41 (dense_low_card_high).

proposals.name: Length-economy relative to implied difficulty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer reaches its conclusion in only one or two short paragraphs even though the question posed is nontrivial. Score 0 if the answer sprawls across many paragraphs, multiple sub-derivations, or several stages of exposition to reach (or fail to reach) its conclusion.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R13 are one- or two-line responses (dense_high_card_low, dense_pct .814 and .790), while R38 and R44 (dense_low_card_high) run to many long paragraphs of exposition for comparable or lesser technical payoff.

proposals.name: Explicit treatment of edge cases or exceptions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly carves out and analyzes special or degenerate cases (e.g. a zero ring, an empty set, a boundary index, a sign ambiguity) that qualify or limit an otherwise general claim. Score 0 if the answer states a general claim or method with no discussion of exceptions or boundary conditions.
proposals.rationale: R12 carefully treats the zero-ring edge case, R41 splits into Case 1 (m=0) and Case 2 (m>0) with further sub-cases, and R60 notes epsilon 'can be positive or negative or even null' -- all three are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard rewards this completeness more than dense does.

proposals.name: Visible revision markers within the answer text
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer text contains explicit revision markers such as 'Edit:', 'EDIT 1', 'EDIT 2', or 'Update:' indicating it was appended to or revised after an initial version. Score 0 if the answer reads as a single unrevised pass with no such markers.
proposals.rationale: R04 contains an explicit 'Edit:' section responding to further reader confusion, and R41 contains 'EDIT 1' and 'EDIT 2' sections responding to a named commenter; both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting visible iterative revision correlates with scorecard reward but not with what dense perceives.

proposals.name: Final line restates the exact target expression asked for
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer's last displayed result explicitly mirrors the specific expression, number, or option format requested in the question (e.g. the question asks to show X=Y and the final line literally states X=Y, or the question is multiple-choice and the answer names the option letter). Score 0 if the answer's conclusion is generic and never ties back to the exact form the question asked for.
proposals.rationale: R34's final line reproduces the question's target expression '2π log(4/3)/3' verbatim, and R09 and R18 both close with 'Option (A) is correct' / '(A)' matching the multiple-choice framing of their shared question; all three are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Dismisses other answers as overcomplicated
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer contains language explicitly dismissing other posted answers or approaches as unnecessarily complex or wrong while asserting its own approach is simpler or more direct (e.g. 'the other answers are way too complicated', 'you are overcomplicating it'). Score 0 if the answer contains no comparative or critical language about other answers.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('The other answers are way too complicated for this particular problem... they're completely overkill here') and R58 ('You are overcomplicating it. Look at this quickly') both use this dismissive-comparative framing and are, notably, dense_low_card_high -- suggesting overt criticism of other answers does not track what the dense model perceives as acceptance-worthy.

proposals.name: Opens by directly explaining the named notation or object
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the opening sentences of the answer directly define or explain the exact term, notation, or object referenced in the question, with no unrelated setup beforehand. Score 0 if the answer opens with tangential material, general background, or commentary before addressing the specific thing the question named.
proposals.rationale: R23 opens with 'The notation C^x is the multiplicative group consisting of all of the nonzero elements of C' directly answering a notation question, and R25 opens with 'You are summing n terms, all equal to a' directly addressing the summation property asked about; both are dense_high_card_low (R23 has the single highest dense_pct in the slice, .991).

proposals.name: States an explicit verdict in the first sentence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the very first sentence of the answer delivers a direct verdict to a yes/no, true/false, or correct/incorrect-shaped question (e.g. 'This is not possible', 'Your DFA looks good to me', 'No, ...'). Score 0 if any verdict only emerges after substantial setup, or the answer never states an explicit verdict at all.
proposals.rationale: R27 opens with 'This is not possible. One way to show this is the following' and R33 opens with 'Your DFA looks good to me', both delivering an immediate up-front verdict before any supporting work; both rows are dense_high_card_low, unlike R01 or R38 (dense_low_card_high) which build up over many paragraphs before any resolution.

proposals.name: Presupposes prior answers already posted
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how strongly the answer's opening and framing language presupposes that OTHER answers to the same question already exist and have been read by the writer (e.g., phrases like 'another approach', 'yet another way', 'the other answer', explicit reference to a previously-posted answer or its author, 'to add to what has been said', 'just for completeness'). 0 = the answer addresses the question as if it were the first/only response, with no acknowledgment of other answers; 10 = the answer opens by explicitly framing itself as an addition/alternative/complement to previously-existing answers. Do not judge whether this framing makes the answer better or worse -- score only the extent of the presupposition, present or absent.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('Another approach:'), R11 ('Here is an another proof...'), R13 ('Yet another approach.'), R17 ('Here is yet another way...'), R28 ('Along the same lines as the other answer...'), R36 ('The other answer has roughly the right idea...'), R39 ('The case p=2 was done in the other answer...'), R45 ('a complement to the Robert Israel's answer'), R49 ('The other answers are way too complicated...'), R56 ('This second answer gives a shorter proof...') are almost all dense_low_card_high, while dense_high_card_low rows R09, R16, R18, R19, R22 show none of this framing -- late-arriving, self-consciously-additional answers track the scorecard signal, not necessarily asker acceptance.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (posted after other answers already existed)

proposals.name: Era-marked legacy LaTeX notation
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much OLD-STYLE / legacy LaTeX notation appears in the math typesetting (e.g., \Bbb{} instead of \mathbb{}, \frak{} instead of \mathfrak{}, \cal{} instead of \mathcal{}, hand-rolled \def/\newcommand macro redefinitions in place of standard commands). 0 = no such legacy notation is present (only modern standard commands, or no notation at all); 10 = pervasive use of these older-style macros throughout the mathematical typesetting. Do not judge whether the notation choice is good practice -- score only how much of it is present.
proposals.rationale: R29 and R55/R56 use \Bbb and \frak (e.g. '2^\frak{c}', '\Bbb Z') and are dense_low_card_high; R13 builds a hand-rolled \def\fitch macro system for its whole proof. By contrast short dense_high_card_low rows R03 and R06 use only plain modern inline math with no legacy macros -- an orthographic-era tell unrelated to whether the asker accepted the post.
proposals.upstream_parent: era of the site's typesetting conventions the answerer learned/practices in

proposals.name: Post-hoc revision/edit markers
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much of the answer text is explicitly marked as having been added or changed after an initial version (e.g., 'EDIT:', 'EDIT 1', 'EDIT 2', 'Update:', text that visibly responds to a named commenter's follow-up). 0 = no revision markers anywhere; 10 = the answer is substantially built from multiple labeled edit/update segments. Do not judge whether the edits improved the answer -- score only the presence and extent of revision markers.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('EDIT / After a long calculation...'), R49 ('Edit: ... or I'll just do it for you myself...'), and R50 ('EDIT 1... EDIT 2... To @ Asaf Shachar...') are all dense_low_card_high and show heavy edit-marker structure, while terse dense_high_card_low rows R51 and R42 show none -- a revision-history tell rather than an acceptance signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission/engagement timing (answer was revised over an extended period after initial posting)

proposals.name: Named-peer citation of other site users
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the answer explicitly names or addresses another specific person (a commenter, another answerer, a professor, or a handle/username, e.g. 'Bill', 'Ted', '@supinf', 'Robert Israel', 'Prof. Shifrin', 'Asaf Shachar') as part of crediting, correcting, or replying to them. 0 = no other individual is named or addressed anywhere; 10 = the answer is structured substantially around naming and responding to a specific other person. Do not judge whether the crediting is appropriate or the response is correct -- score only how much naming/addressing of other individuals occurs.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('as suggested by Ted'), R08 ('expanding on a comment by Bill'), R14 ('@iam_agf has the other'), R43 ('@supinf showed us a nice set of examples'), and R50 ('To @ Asaf Shachar') are all dense_low_card_high; dense_high_card_low rows R09, R16, R34 name no one -- a marker of a socially-networked, conversational answerer rather than of asker acceptance.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's social embeddedness / standing and relationships within the site's community

proposals.name: Terse confirmation without full derivation
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the answer consists of a short, flatly declarative confirmation or hint rather than a worked-through derivation (e.g., 'Your computation looks fine.', 'Your DFA looks good to me.', a bare 'Hint:' followed by one or two lines). 0 = the answer is a full step-by-step derivation with no terse unelaborated verdict; 10 = the entire answer is a terse verdict/hint with essentially no elaboration. Do not judge whether brevity is a virtue -- score only the extent of terse, unelaborated phrasing.
proposals.rationale: R51 ('Your computation looks fine. I don't think there is an easier way to proceed.') and R32/R18 (bare 'Hint:' fragments) are dense_high_card_low; longer worked-out dense_low_card_high rows R05 and R39 show essentially none of this terse-verdict register -- a stylistic register tell distinct from correctness.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practiced terseness / seniority-signaled confidence in the format

proposals.name: External resource/citation apparatus
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the answer cites or points to resources outside the immediate derivation -- named external tools ('WolframAlpha'), databases ('OEIS'), hyperlinked source material, or a formal reference list with author names, journal names, or DOI links. 0 = no external resources or citations are mentioned; 10 = the answer contains multiple such citations or a formal bibliography. Do not judge whether the citations are relevant or well-chosen -- score only how much citation apparatus is present.
proposals.rationale: R23 ('consult the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences... A038534') and R27 (a three-item numbered bibliography with journal names and DOI links) are both dense_high_card_low despite heavy citation apparatus, while R10 ('try using WolframAlpha for basic integrals') is dense_low_card_high with a passing citation -- citation-apparatus density does not cleanly track either model and is a plausible confound needing discount in both directions.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice of resourcefulness/scholarly formatting in the format

proposals.name: Custom macro / boxed-answer markup density
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much specialized LaTeX markup machinery is used beyond ordinary inline formulas -- custom \def/\newcommand macros, \begin{align} multi-line derivation blocks, boxed or framed final answers (\boxed{}, \bbox[...]{}, \fbox{}), or hand-built array/diagram environments. 0 = only plain inline math with no such machinery; 10 = extensive custom macros, aligned multi-line blocks, and boxed/framed elements throughout. Do not judge whether the markup is well-executed -- score only how much of this markup machinery is present.
proposals.rationale: R05 defines \newcommand{Dom}{...}\newcommand{Rng}{...} and R13 builds a full custom \def\fitch proof-tree macro (both dense_low_card_high), while R59 uses \bbox[...]{...} framed boxes and R44 ends in a \boxed{} final answer (both dense_high_card_low) -- markup-machinery density cuts across both slices and is a formatting-practice tell, not an acceptance signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's typographic/markup habit and practiced fluency with the site's formatting conventions

proposals.name: Question genre framed as routine computation vs. conceptual discussion
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the answer's own opening frames the attached question as a routine, closed-form computation with a single numeric or symbolic target (as opposed to an open-ended conceptual or opinion-inviting discussion) -- e.g., immediately restating a formula to manipulate, working toward one boxed number, or referencing multiple-choice options. 0 = the answer treats the question as open-ended/conceptual, weighing interpretations or definitions; 10 = the answer treats it as a closed computational exercise with a single target value from the first line. Do not judge whether that framing is correct for the question -- score only how strongly the answer's own framing leans toward routine computation.
proposals.rationale: R16, R34, and R48 are three independent answers to the identical routine multiple-choice question 'The sum of the factors of 9!', each ending in a single boxed numeral or 'Option (A) is correct', and all three are dense_high_card_low; by contrast R24 ('The importance of parallel arrows...') and R31 ('Why constant symbols...') are open conceptual discussions and both dense_low_card_high -- question genre is a topic-level confound, not evidence of asker choice.
proposals.upstream_parent: kind of question the answer is attached to (routine homework computation vs. conceptual/discussion-drawing question)

proposals.name: Raw answer length / verbosity
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate the sheer length of the answer text (word/line count, number of displayed equations, number of paragraphs) relative to the range seen in this set, independent of content. 0 = extremely short (one or two lines); 10 = extremely long, multi-paragraph with many displayed equations. Do not judge whether the length is warranted by the problem's difficulty -- score only the raw extent of the text.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R39 are very long multi-paragraph derivations (dense_low_card_high, card_pct=.974/.955), while R03 and R06 are one-line/two-line answers (dense_high_card_low, dense_pct=.918/.883) -- raw length is a strong surface proxy that plausibly drives scorecard aggregation (more criteria find something to score) independent of asker preference.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Author personality / conversational asides
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much informal, conversational, or humorous personal voice appears in the prose -- exclamations, jokes, emoticons, self-deprecating asides, a personal sign-off name, or direct colloquial address to the reader (e.g., 'Well, jolly gosh!', '^_^', 'Cheers! -Shahar', 'I hope this was helpful'). 0 = strictly impersonal, formal register throughout; 10 = pervasive informal/conversational personal voice. Do not judge whether the informality is charming or unprofessional -- score only how much of it is present.
proposals.rationale: R10 ('Well, jolly gosh! ... Cheers! -Shahar') and R23 ('I hope this helps ^_^') are both dense_low_card_high, while R54 ('I hope this was helpful') is dense_high_card_low -- conversational voice appears on both sides of the split and is a personality tell, not an acceptance signal, so it must be discounted from both models symmetrically.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's personal communicative practice/register

proposals.name: Stands as primary resolution, not a supplementary alternative
proposals.instruction: Score how far the answer presents itself as THE resolution of the question rather than as one more entry in an existing pile. 10 = the text opens by engaging the question or the asker directly and never signals that other answers already exist; a reader would take it as the (or a first) response. 5 = neutral framing with a single passing nod to other material. 0 = the answer is explicitly framed as an addition or variant: openers such as 'Another approach', 'Here is yet another way', 'Along the same lines as the other answer', 'This is expanding on a comment by X', 'I post this answer separately', 'This is not an answer to the question but a complement to ...'. Judge only the framing, not the mathematics.
proposals.rationale: This is the single most visible surface split in the slice. Nearly every dense_low_card_high row announces itself as an alternative: R09 ('Here is an another proof'), R14 ('Yet another approach'), R16 ('Along the same lines as the other answer'), R26 ('Another approach'), R38 ('Here is more standard way'), R43 ('Another option'), R47 ('This second answer gives a shorter proof'), R52 ('Here is yet another way, in case you are interested'), R57 ('The other answers are way too complicated'). The dense_high_card_low rows (R03, R20, R21, R28) carry no such framing. A scorecard reading for rigor and completeness cannot see this framing at all, while a single asker choosing among answers to their own question is reading exactly it.

proposals.name: Explicit verdict on the asker's own posted work
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer adjudicates the asker's own attempt. 10 = the answer states a clear verdict on what the asker did ('your work is correct', 'your DFA looks good', 'your computation looks fine', 'there may be some little mistakes in your computation') and, where a fault is found, says where. 5 = the asker's attempt is mentioned but not adjudicated. 0 = the answer never engages the asker's attempt at all, presenting only its own independent development. Score the presence and directness of the verdict, not whether the verdict is right.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('So your work is correct'), R13 ('Your DFA looks good to me'), R24 ('It should be used. There may be some little mistakes in your computation'), and R59 ('Your computation looks fine. I don't think there is an easier way') are all dense-high with very low card percentiles (R59 card=0.051, R24 card=0.024) — the scorecard sees almost no mathematical content because the content is a verdict. R59 in particular is two sentences and nothing else, yet the dense model ranks it at 0.790. By contrast R18, R36, R47 never touch the asker's attempt and sit at dense 0.084/0.097/0.148.

proposals.name: Diagnoses the asker's error and stops there
proposals.instruction: Composite. Score jointly (a) whether the answer locates a specific defect in the ASKER's own reasoning, stated in the asker's own terms and notation, and (b) whether it stops once that defect and its repair are stated. 10 = pinpoints the exact wrong step or missing case in the asker's method and closes within a few lines of doing so. 5 = diagnoses the asker's error but then continues into a long general exposition well past the repair, or diagnoses only vaguely. 0 = diagnoses no defect in the asker's reasoning at all, or the defect diagnosed belongs to another answer rather than to the asker.
proposals.rationale: R03 is the pure case: it tells the asker exactly which factor is missing from their numerator terms and which scenario their method fails to count, in their own notation, in two short paragraphs — dense 0.952 against card 0.187. R33 also opens with a precise diagnosis of the asker's error (real vs complex cube-root function) but then runs on through two philosophical viewpoints and a dozen displayed lines: dense 0.227, card 0.985. R17 diagnoses carefully but the target is 'the other answer', not the asker: dense 0.269. The (b) clause and the whose-error clause are what a length-and-rigor scorecard inverts.

proposals.name: Length proportionate to the difficulty of the question
proposals.instruction: Composite. First judge the difficulty of the QUESTION on its own (routine calculus/algebra/counting exercise vs. genuinely hard or research-level). Then score the match. 10 = a routine question answered in a compact, complete unit, or a hard question answered at the length the hard question actually requires. 5 = mild mismatch. 0 = severe over-expansion: a modest or routine question answered with multiple screens of displayed formalism, sectioning, or general theory the question did not ask for. Penalize only expansion the question does not need; do not penalize length that the question demands.
proposals.rationale: R28 (simplify 2*2^45 + 6*2^45) is five lines and dense 0.867 / card 0.121; R56 ('Property of summation') is two lines and dense 0.918 / card 0.316; R04 answers 'Series equal to an integral' in one displayed chain, dense 0.883 / card 0.257. Against these, R10 answers a clarification request about the mechanics of the tensor product with a multi-screen reorganization (dense 0.910 is the exception, but note its card is only 0.207), and R36 answers a function-analysis question with a full Fourier-series development plus plots and a disclaimer, dense 0.097 / card 0.994. A criterion bank scoring thoroughness rewards the expansion; the asker of a small question is not buying it.

proposals.name: Free of dependence on other users' contributions
proposals.instruction: Score how self-contained the answer is with respect to the site conversation around it. 10 = no reference to any other user, commenter, or answerer by name or handle; the answer's argument stands on its own. 5 = one incidental acknowledgement that does not carry the argument. 0 = the answer is built on, credits, corrects, or continues another named participant's contribution ('as suggested by Ted', 'expanding on a comment by Bill', '@supinf showed us ...', 'a complement to Robert Israel's answer', 'Clive's answer is already a good one'). Named references to published literature or textbooks do NOT count — only references to participants in this thread.
proposals.rationale: Every row in this slice that names a fellow participant is dense-low and card-high: R11 (Bill, dense 0.223 / card 0.975), R18 (Ted, 0.084 / 0.917), R22 ('EDIT 1. (To Asaf Shachar)', 0.341 / 0.993), R27 ('@supinf showed us a nice set of examples', 0.134 / 0.822), R34 ('a complement to the Robert Israel's answer', 0.027 / 0.959), R36 ('Semiclassical got there first', 0.097 / 0.994), R49 ('Clive's answer is already a good one', 0.116 / 0.766), R10 ('now validated by Prof. Shifrin'). Meanwhile R20 cites Rudin theorem 12.29 and R46 cites the OEIS, both dense-high — which is why the criterion must exclude literature citations. The scorecard reads these acknowledgements as scholarly care; the dense model reads them as 'this answer is a footnote to the thread'.

proposals.name: Delivers a resolution rather than commentary about the question
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer actually resolves what was asked. 10 = the answer produces the thing the question asked for — the value, the proof, the construction, the definition, the decision — and hands it over. 5 = the answer supplies a partial resolution plus substantial commentary. 0 = the answer principally comments on, reframes, qualifies, or deflates the question rather than answering it: caveats about why the question is less interesting than it looks, disclaimers that this is not an answer, or discussion of what a cited author must have meant.
proposals.rationale: R34 states outright 'This is not an answer to the question but a complement to the Robert Israel's answer' (dense 0.027 / card 0.959); R55 argues the asked-about phenomenon has 'less than meets the eye' and concludes 'the importance of parallel arrows in commutative squares? In general...none' (0.076 / 0.838); R25 supplies an important caveat about non-uniqueness rather than the requested construction (0.096 / 0.801); R08 spends its first half adjudicating what Dr. Stewart meant in a 1996 book (0.104 / 0.848). Contrast R23, which drives to '$(-\infty,-7]\cup[-5,+\infty)$. Done!' (0.903 / 0.086) and R21, which kills the claim with a three-line counterexample (0.740 / 0.032). A criterion bank rewards nuance and caveating; a resolution is what a single asker was after.

proposals.name: Actionable next step handed to a visibly working asker
proposals.instruction: Composite. Judge (a) whether the question shows an asker actively working a problem (a stated attempt, an exercise, a stuck step) and (b) whether the answer hands that asker something they can immediately execute — the name of the theorem to apply, the substitution to make, the reference to look up, the concrete unlock. 10 = clearly a working asker AND a precise, executable unlock, even if the answer is short and leaves the labor to them. 5 = an unlock that is present but vague, or a complete solution to a question where no attempt was shown. 0 = nothing the asker could act on: the answer either performs the whole task in a register the asker could not have produced, or gestures without specifying anything executable.
proposals.rationale: Short hint-shaped answers are dense-high and card-floor throughout this slice: R12 ('Hint: Apply Melanaus theorem in ...', dense 0.768 / card 0.035), R54 ('Hint:' plus four lines reducing to tan x = -1, 0.814 / 0.018), R06 ('Hint: ... a disguised version of the Schroder-Bernstein theorem', 0.931 / 0.339), R39 ('The following may get you started', 0.922 / 0.052), R46 (points the asker at OEIS A038534 and stops, 0.789 / 0.041). Rubric banks reliably score hints as incomplete; this criterion is the direct counterweight, and it is exactly the 'what the scorecard misses' direction.

proposals.name: Impersonal exposition, not authorial self-presentation
proposals.instruction: Score how far the answer keeps its author out of view. 10 = fully impersonal or minimally first-person; nothing about the author's plans, corpus, preferences, or process. 5 = light first-person hedging ('I think', 'if I remember right'). 0 = conspicuous authorial presence: announcements of the author's other posts or forthcoming writing, notes on why this was posted separately, signatures, personal taste claims about which proof the author finds nicer, or disclaimers about the author's priority.
proposals.rationale: R15 ('I want to record here what can be done ... I have a plan for a much larger blog post', dense 0.232 / card 0.955), R36 ('I post this answer separately, so that the analytics are not lost among the illustrative material from my first post' plus a priority 'Disclaimer', 0.097 / 0.994), R10 ('ATTEMPT TO ORGANIZE THIS MATERIAL (now validated by Prof. Shifrin - at least in part; errors, mine)', card 0.207), R09 ('which I find easier to understand ... more intuitive I find', 0.021 / 0.671), R02 (signed '-Shahar', 0.077 / 0.788). Distinct from A05: this is about the author's own presence, not credit to others. Rubric banks are indifferent to it; a reader deciding whether an answer was written for them is not.

proposals.name: Respectful, non-condescending stance toward the asker
proposals.instruction: Score the tone directed at the asker. 10 = neutral or warm: takes the asker's difficulty seriously, offers help without status display, may close with an offer of further help. 5 = brisk but not disparaging. 0 = belittling: tells the asker they are overcomplicating a triviality, disparages other answers as 'overkill', instructs the asker to go use a computer algebra site next time, or implies the asker has failed to look for a few seconds. Score the stance only, independent of correctness.
proposals.rationale: R02 combines a clean correct u-substitution with 'You are overcomplicating it', 'Well, jolly gosh!', and 'For future, try using WolframAlpha for basic integrals. Cheers!' — dense 0.077 against card 0.788, one of the sharpest inversions in the slice. R57 opens 'The other answers are way too complicated ... completely overkill here', then 'Just look at this equation for a few seconds' and 'since you seem to think it leads to another recurrence...': dense 0.043 / card 0.863. Compare the warm closers in dense-high rows: R42 ('I hope this was helpful') at 0.981 and R46 ('I hope this helps ^_^') at 0.789. Tone is invisible to a correctness-and-rigor bank and highly visible to the person who asked.

proposals.name: Reaches a clean terminus with no unresolved residue
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer arrives somewhere and stops. 10 = the answer lands on an explicit final object — a value, a boxed result, a closed set, a qed — with no admitted gaps and no hedged recollection. 5 = it lands but with minor loose ends. 0 = the answer ends in admitted incompleteness or hedged memory: 'if I remember right', 'I proved only that ... has at least one solution', results the author calls debatable, or a closing complaint that the standard treatment is wrong.
proposals.rationale: R11 rests a step on 'Now, if I remember right, the Jensen inequality for Log reads ...' (dense 0.223 / card 0.975); R22 concedes in EDIT 1 that 'I proved only that the equation f(x)=1 has at least one solution' before a later patch (0.341 / 0.993); R34 offers two further envelope solutions and calls them 'discutable' (0.027 / 0.959); R08 ends on 'But I have a problem with the common description of the hyperwebster' (0.104 / 0.848). Against these, R23 closes '$(-\infty,-7]\cup[-5,+\infty)$ ... Done!' (0.903), R29 assembles to the exact requested closed form (0.899), and R30 ends 'you can conlude that $U_k$ is countable' (0.807). Scorecards credit displayed machinery whether or not it terminates.

proposals.name: Single composed answer, not an edit-accreted thread reply
proposals.instruction: Score the compositional integrity of the text. 10 = one coherent piece written through, no visible revision scars. 5 = one appended clarification. 0 = layered accretion: multiple 'EDIT'/'EDIT 2' blocks, blocks addressed to named third parties, or an appendix conceding a point and re-doing the argument. Judge the structure of the text, not the quality of the added content.
proposals.rationale: R22 carries 'EDIT 1. (To Asaf Shachar)' and 'EDIT 2. To @ Asaf Shachar. Now I prove (with the help of a colleague) ...' — dense 0.341 / card 0.993. R11 has an 'EDIT / After a long calculation' block (0.223 / 0.975); R57's 'Edit: or I'll just do it for you myself, since you seem to think ...' (0.043 / 0.863); R35's trailing 'edit:' clause (0.130 / 0.796). Edit layers are evidence the answer's life happened in a debate with commenters rather than with the person who asked; a bank scoring completeness reads the same layers as added rigor.

proposals.name: Bounded personal question answered in the asker's register
proposals.instruction: Composite. Judge (a) whether the QUESTION is a bounded, asker-specific one — a computation to finish, a notation to decode, an attempt to check, a small counting or algebra exercise — as opposed to a broad, community-interest or research-level prompt; and (b) whether the answer is pitched at the level the asker is plainly working at. 10 = bounded personal question, answered squarely at the asker's level with no machinery beyond what the asker could follow. 5 = one of the two conditions holds. 0 = a broad scholarly prompt answered as a contribution to the literature, with the answer aimed at expert readers generally rather than at the person who asked.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high end of this slice is dominated by bounded personal prompts answered in kind: 'Differentiate y=e^{ax^3}' (R07, 0.859), 'How to simplify expression with exponents?' (R28, 0.867), 'Property of summation' (R56, 0.918), 'Set of complex numbers notation' (R05, 0.991), 'Is there an efficient way to add minutes in your head?' (R42, 0.981). The dense-low/card-high end is dominated by broad prompts answered as scholarship: 'Constructive Proof of Kronecker-Weber?' (R15, 0.232), 'Euler Characteristic of fiber bundle using Differential Geometry' (R18, 0.084), 'Mathematical statement with simple independence proof from ZF' (R60, 0.323), 'Is the subset of symmetric 3x3 matrices with given eigenvalues a manifold?' (R47, 0.148). The question half of the item is doing real work that a text-quality bank scoring only the answer cannot use.

proposals.name: Key move visible in the opening lines
proposals.instruction: Score how quickly a reader sees the decisive idea. 10 = the resolving move — the substitution, the counterexample, the theorem invoked, the identification of the mistake — is apparent within roughly the first two lines or the first display. 5 = it appears after moderate setup. 0 = the decisive move is reachable only after extensive preliminary construction, definitions, or notation macros, so that a reader must work through most of the text before knowing what the answer is doing.
proposals.rationale: R21 puts the whole disproof in its first display: 'Let A = R^inf, B = R, C = R^2' (dense 0.740 / card 0.032). R04 is a single chain from integral to series (0.883 / 0.257). R20 names the mechanism in its second sentence (0.874 / 0.122). Against these, R47 sets up an equivariant orbit map, a stabilizer computation, and two applications of a lemma before the manifold claim lands (0.148 / 0.976), and R36 develops logs, Taylor expansion, and theta functions before any statement about the function (0.097 / 0.994). Front-loading is precisely the property a per-criterion rubric averaging over content cannot register.

proposals.name: Names the idea in words alongside the symbols
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer says in plain language why its move works, not merely that it works. 10 = the governing idea is named in prose the asker can carry away ('you need to multiply by the birthdays of everyone who does not match'; 'carrying is by 60 instead of 10'; 'avoiding the largest cipher gives uniqueness of representation'). 5 = brief motivating remarks around a mostly symbolic derivation. 0 = pure symbol-pushing or a bare formal object with no prose account of the idea driving it.
proposals.rationale: R14 is an enormous Fitch-style natural-deduction diagram with a single line of prose (dense 0.044 / card 0.732) and R26 is a bare numbered list of premises and detachments with no motivating word (0.006 / 0.738) — the two lowest dense percentiles in the slice, on the same question. The prose-carrying answers run high: R42 explains base-60 carrying in words and even sets a practice exercise (0.981), R30 explains why the (k+1)-nary map avoids the 0.4999... collision (0.807), R50 explains the pushforward-of-measure intuition and adds an anti-example (0.960). A judge scoring formal correctness credits R14 and R26 fully; the asker gets nothing portable from either.

proposals.name: Substance not inflated by typographic apparatus
proposals.instruction: Score the ratio of substantive content to presentational apparatus. 10 = whatever mathematical content is present is delivered plainly, without formatting doing work the content does not — plain text, ordinary displays, no sectioning beyond need. 0 = heavy apparatus (custom macros, aligned multi-page displays, section headers, numbered claims and lemmas, reference lists, figure callouts) wrapping a contribution that is derivative, partial, or narrow relative to its bulk. Score the apparatus-to-substance ratio, not the presence of formatting or the elegance of the typesetting.
proposals.rationale: This is the clearest 'what the scorecard over-credits' axis. R14's \def\fitch macro and nested boxed derivation reach card 0.732 at dense 0.044; R47's numbered claims and displayed equivariance argument reach card 0.976 at dense 0.148; R15's macro block, boxed theorem statement, and 'Claim 1 / Claim 2' scaffolding reach card 0.955 at dense 0.232; R36 adds figure callouts, a Wolfram confirmation, and a disclaimer for card 0.994 at dense 0.097. Symmetrically, the plainest texts in the slice sit at the card floor while the dense model ranks them high: R41 is unformatted prose arithmetic with a garbled parenthetical (card 0.004 / dense 0.834), R51 is a one-line list of candidates (card 0.005 / dense 0.742), R19 is a bare inequality chain (card 0.023 / dense 0.816).

proposals.name: Deixis presupposing other answers already exist
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer's text presupposes that other answers to the same question already exist. Count explicit phrases ('the other answer', 'the other answers', 'as suggested above', 'my first post', 'my 2011 answer') and ordinal/alternative framings that position this text as an addition to a set ('another approach', 'yet another way', 'here is a second thing', 'this second answer', 'a complement to', 'I post this separately', 'expanding on a comment', 'here is more standard way'). 0 = the text engages the raw question from scratch with no sign that anything has been said yet; 10 = the opening sentence itself is built entirely around already-existing answers or the author's own earlier post.
