Score only how much such presupposing language is present. Do NOT judge whether the answer is good, correct, useful, or well written, and do NOT reward or penalise politeness toward other answerers.
proposals.rationale: Arrival position is not the asker's choice, but it is heavily fingerprinted here and appears to track the split: R01 opens 'Along the same lines as the other answer', R20 opens 'This is not an answer to the question but a complement to the Robert Israel's answer', R37 opens 'The other answers are way too complicated', R57 opens 'This second answer gives a shorter proof' -- while R15, R22, R28, R40 address the bare question with no such marker at all. Tagged mixed because an answerer who has read the earlier answers can genuinely close a residual gap (R30 corrects edge cases the other answer missed).
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (how many answers had already been posted when this one arrived)

proposals.name: Named or @-handled address of other site participants
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text names or addresses specific other people on the site: @-handles, user names, first names, honorifics of other participants, or direct second-person reply to a named interlocutor, and references to 'the OP' as a third party. 0 = no person other than the writer and a generic 'you' is referred to; 10 = named participants appear repeatedly and structure the text (e.g. sections addressed to a named user). Count the presence of such naming only. Do NOT judge whether the credit is deserved, gracious, or relevant, and do NOT judge the mathematics.
proposals.rationale: Naming other users is a trace of thread-level social activity, not of anything the asker's own selection is supposed to measure. It is dense in R03 ('@iam_agf has the other'), R47 ('EDIT 2. To @ Asaf Shachar'), R50 ("Clive's answer is already a good one"), R58 ('@supinf showed us a nice set of examples'), R44 ("as in @ReihardMeier's answer"), R56 ('as suggested by Ted'), and absent from R15, R23, R28, R40. Purely a nuisance parent: who else happened to be in the thread.
proposals.upstream_parent: social/conversation dynamics in the comment thread and the author's embeddedness in the site's regular community

proposals.name: Visible revision scars and appended amendment blocks
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text carries visible marks of having been revised or appended to after first posting: literal markers such as 'EDIT', 'Edit:', 'EDIT 1', 'EDIT 2', 'edit:', 'Disclaimer', 'Note added', 'To clarify my comments above', 'Update', plus blocks that continue the argument after an apparent ending or that answer an objection raised elsewhere. 0 = a single uninterrupted composition with no amendment marker; 10 = multiple explicitly labelled amendment blocks. Score only the visible presence of amendment structure. Do NOT judge whether the amendments improve the answer and do NOT judge correctness.
proposals.rationale: The number of editing rounds is an unseen process variable that leaves a hard textual fingerprint. R47 carries two labelled blocks ('EDIT 1. (To Asaf Shachar)', 'EDIT 2.'), R37 has 'Edit: or I'll just do it for you myself', R36 has 'EDIT / After a long calculation', R41 has 'EDIT: I have three suggestions', R04 ends with a 'Disclaimer' paragraph, R44 opens 'To clarify my comments above'; R15, R34, R38, R40 have none. Tagged mixed because rounds of editing can genuinely strengthen an answer.
proposals.upstream_parent: post-hoc editing under comment pressure, and the amount of elapsed dwell time the author spent on the post after publishing

proposals.name: Site-veteran markup habits: macro preambles, tags, spoilers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of practised site-specific markup machinery in the text: inline TeX macro preambles defined at the top of the post (\def, \newcommand, \DeclareMathOperator), numbered equation tagging and cross-referencing (\tag, \label, \eqref, '(1)', '($\ast$)'), hand-built array/aligned/cases scaffolding, boxed or highlighted output, colour commands, spoiler-hidden content ('a full proof is hidden below'), and explicit sectioning or named Claim/Definition/Proof headers. 0 = plain prose with at most simple inline math; 10 = a macro preamble plus tagged, cross-referenced, sectioned apparatus. Score only how much of this apparatus is present. Do NOT judge whether it is used tastefully or whether the formatting aids the reader.
proposals.rationale: Fluent markup is a habit of long practice on the site, an unseen author attribute, yet it is fully visible: R10 opens with '\def\fitch', R13 with '\def\QQ\def\ZZ\def\Gal' plus Claim/Proof sectioning, R53 with '\newcommand{Dom}', R57 with '\newcommand{\O}', R11 uses \tag/\label/\eqref throughout, R16 uses the hidden-proof convention; R21 and R32 are typed as plain text with none of it. Tagged mixed because practised writers plausibly also write genuinely better answers.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's practice and standing in this format (a high-reputation site regular versus a first-time poster)

proposals.name: Residue of stripped images and external tool citations
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text refers to material that is not present in the text itself: sentences pointing at a plot, diagram, illustration, map, keypad, or 'the figure below' with no figure following; dangling link anchors rendered as bare words ('source 1', 'source 2', 'see this link', 'this post', 'linked above in the comments'); and citations of external computation or reference tools (Wolfram Alpha, WA, OEIS sequence numbers, DOIs, textbook theorem numbers, journal reference lists). 0 = the text is fully self-contained with no reference to absent material or outside tools; 10 = the argument repeatedly leans on illustrations or links that the reader cannot see here. Score only the amount of such reference-to-absent-material. Do NOT judge whether the missing material would have helped, and do NOT treat citing sources as good or bad practice.
proposals.rationale: This is a scraping-and-tooling artifact, not the asker's judgement, but it is highly visible and unevenly distributed: R04 says 'Here is an illustration for $a=1$' and 'This result is confirmed by Wolfram Alpha' with nothing rendered, R20 says 'The map drawn below shows the curves' and cites 'given by WA', R05 says 'the plot below shows histograms', R08 ends in bare 'source 1 / source 2', R54 points to an OEIS id, R52 appends three DOI references, R39 says 'Please see comment below for more info on these diagrams'. Nuisance parent throughout.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's authoring toolchain (plotting software, computer algebra, reference managers) interacting with the corpus pipeline that strips embedded media and link targets

proposals.name: Second-person diagnosis of the asker's own attempt
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text is addressed to the asker's own work rather than expounding for a general reader: possessive references to the asker's attempt ('your computation', 'your method', 'your DFA', 'your work is correct', 'what you did'), verdicts on that attempt, second-person imperatives about what 'you need to' do next, and interpretation of what the asker meant. 0 = fully third-person or first-person-plural exposition that never mentions the asker's attempt; 10 = the whole text is a point-by-point response to the asker's own steps. Score only the extent of asker-directed framing. Do NOT judge whether the diagnosis is correct or kind.
proposals.rationale: Whom the answer is written for is an unseen stance with a clean fingerprint, and it separates the slice: R34 is only 'Your computation looks fine', R14 is 'If you are enumerating everyone's birthday... your method isn't counting', R17 'There may be some little mistakes in your computation', R55 'So your work is correct', R41 'Your DFA looks good to me', R43 ends 'Done!' after fixing the asker's route -- while R27, R53, R57, R60 are audience-facing expositions that never mention an attempt. Tagged mixed because directly addressing the asker's confusion may genuinely serve them.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's relationship to the reader (writing for this one asker versus for the audience of future searchers)

proposals.name: Sheer bulk and display-mathematics density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of textual bulk and displayed-equation density, judged on volume alone: total length, number of separate display-math blocks and multi-line aligned environments, number of paragraph breaks, and presence of multi-stage derivation chains. 0 = one or two sentences with at most one displayed line; 10 = many screens of prose interleaved with a dozen or more display blocks. Count volume only, exactly as a word- and equation-counter would. Do NOT judge whether the length is warranted, whether the derivation is complete, or whether the answer is thorough.
proposals.rationale: A pure size proxy, mechanically computable and therefore an easy shortcut for either model, and it varies by two orders of magnitude across the slice: R15 and R34 are single sentences, R38 is one line, whereas R44, R45, R52, R53 and R13 run to many display blocks and several thousand characters. It must be declared a nuisance so that neither model may bank on length; the asker's choice is not a word count.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Elementary-exercise versus research-register vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the vocabulary and objects in the text belong to advanced or specialist mathematics rather than to routine early-coursework computation. Low scores: arithmetic, factors and divisors, basic differentiation and integration by substitution, elementary trigonometric identities, simple summation identities, textbook probability counting. High scores: named advanced machinery and specialist notation (Galois groups, cyclotomic fields, forcing and generic filters, Poincare-Hopf, Bell polynomials and Faa di Bruno, Jacobi theta functions, spectral theorem on Hilbert space, cardinal arithmetic with $2^{\mathfrak c}$). Score the register of the subject matter only. Do NOT judge difficulty as merit, and do NOT judge whether the answer handles its material well.
proposals.rationale: Subject register is a proxy for the container the answer sits in -- how many rival answers arrived and how the thread was consumed -- rather than for the asker's selection. It splits the slice sharply: R21, R22, R35, R55 are elementary computations, while R13, R53, R56, R57, R52 are graduate/research-level; topic is not merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: the kind of question the answer is attached to (a routine homework computation that one person wants closed versus a conceptual question that draws a crowd of answerers and spectators)

proposals.name: Emotive interjections, exclamation runs, sign-offs and signatures
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of informal affective and personal-closing material: interjections and exclamations ('Well, jolly gosh!', 'AHAAA!', 'Cheers!'), runs of two or more exclamation marks, capitalised shouting, emoticons or kaomoji, closing pleasantries ('I hope this was helpful', 'I hope this helps'), a typed personal signature or initials, self-congratulatory flourishes ('Done!', 'qed', 'and we are done'), and advice about study habits or tooling addressed to the asker as a person. 0 = neutral impersonal register with no affective or closing material; 10 = interjections, exclamation runs and a signed sign-off. Score presence and quantity only. Do NOT judge whether the tone is appropriate, charming, or off-putting.
proposals.rationale: Register is an author trait with no bearing on whether the asker's problem was solved, but it is loudly visible: R06 has 'Well, jolly gosh!', 'Cheers!' and the signature '-Shahar' plus advice to use WolframAlpha, R32 has 'AHAAA!' and 'as our answer!!!!', R42 has 'I hope this was helpful' and 'You try one', R54 ends 'I hope this helps ^_^', R43 ends 'Done!', R56 ends 'qed'; R23, R28, R40 are flatly neutral.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's register habit and inexperience in the format (a newer, more conversational contributor versus a terse practised one)

proposals.name: Withheld completion: hint stance and delegated final steps
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text deliberately stops short of a finished solution: explicit hint framing ('Hint:', 'The following may get you started', 'Here is a sketch'), work handed back to the reader ('now you can solve for $x$', "I'll leave the last step of simplifying to you", 'you try one', 'apply the same reasoning until...'), pointers to a theorem or set of notes the reader must go and use, and answers that terminate mid-derivation by design. 0 = a complete worked argument carried to its stated conclusion; 10 = the text is only a pointer or a first step with the remainder explicitly delegated. Score the extent of withholding only. Do NOT judge whether withholding is pedagogically right or whether the hint is a good one.
proposals.rationale: Hint-stance is a norm-following habit of the answerer rather than a property the asker selects on, and it clusters visibly: R38 is only 'Hint: Apply Melanaus theorem', R35 is 'Hint:' plus two lines ending 'Now you can solve for $x$', R16 opens 'Hint: The statement... is a disguised version of Schroder-Bernstein', R05 opens 'The following may get you started', R37 says "I'll leave the last step of simplifying the summation to you", R41 sends the reader to a colleague's unlinked notes, R42 sets an exercise ('You try one'); R25, R29, R49 carry the computation all the way. Tagged mixed because a well-aimed hint can genuinely be what the asker wanted.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's practice in the format and adherence to site norms about not fully solving apparent homework, plus how quickly the author chose to post

proposals.name: Exact task alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer directly resolves the precise question asked, and 0 when it is mainly tangential, generic, or addresses a different task.
proposals.rationale: R02, R22, and R28 each target the exact requested calculation with almost no detour, unlike answers that broaden or redirect the problem.

proposals.name: Decisive local reduction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one clear observation reduces the problem to a nearly immediate conclusion and the answer applies it correctly; score 0 when no useful reduction is offered.
proposals.rationale: R20 reduces four equal ratios to a single total-sum argument, while R30 identifies the arithmetic-progression structure; R11 similarly points to the critical tangent condition.

proposals.name: Proportionate method choice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method and level of machinery fit the problem’s difficulty and requested scope; score 0 when the response is seriously overcomplicated, underdeveloped, or mismatched.
proposals.rationale: R10 and R36 use elementary methods for elementary tasks, whereas R09 and R43 deploy extensive advanced machinery for highly specialized questions.

proposals.name: Continuity with asker’s approach
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer explicitly adopts and advances the asker’s notation or proposed method; score 0 when it ignores that setup without need.
proposals.rationale: R03 begins from the asker’s second technique, R46 evaluates the asker’s DFA and offers compatible next steps, and R57 works directly from the asker’s computation.

proposals.name: Explicit final conclusion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer clearly states the requested value, set, or classification together with necessary conditions; score 0 when the reader must infer the result or the problem remains unresolved.
proposals.rationale: R07 states the complete solution interval, R12 ends with the requested integral value, and R45 explicitly obtains the fifth-power sum.

proposals.name: Complete proof coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every central inference needed for the claimed result is justified, with 0 for a substantial unsupported leap or merely asserted conclusion.
proposals.rationale: R17 connects the group action, differential, stabilizer, and embedding arguments, while R35 explains the conflicting cube-root manipulations step by step.

proposals.name: Assumption and edge-case care
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer identifies relevant exceptional cases and states domain assumptions explicitly; score 0 when it silently relies on assumptions that can fail.
proposals.rationale: R15 treats zero rings and zero modules, R33 restores omitted solution branches, and R54 notices that multiple matching birthday pairs must also be counted.

proposals.name: Algebraic reliability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when each algebraic, analytic, or numerical transformation is accurate and readily checkable; score 0 when the derivation contains errors, sign problems, or opaque unjustified transformations.
proposals.rationale: The chained calculations in R12 and R50 illustrate checkable algebraic verification, while the compressed estimate in R01 shows why precise transformation reliability matters.

proposals.name: Illuminating examples
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when concrete examples accurately clarify the general idea and its limits; score 0 when examples are absent where useful or are irrelevant or misleading.
proposals.rationale: R27 uses marble orderings to explain induced probability, R40 works several sexagesimal examples, and R58 explains the encoding with periodic expansions.
